rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, Tables 1-2, Fig. 6 - two-year field experiment (2003, 2006) at Harran University farm comparing water pillow (WP) irrigation at three levels with furrow irrigation for soybean; own measurements of yield, soil water content, ET and soil temperature at 20 cm.
rows.notes: The study does measure higher pre-irrigation soil water content (WP1.0 25.5-27.1% vs FI 22.5-23.3%) and higher soil temperature at 20 cm (1.4-2.0 C) under WP than under furrow, but the technology is a patented water-pillow pipe (a 38 cm black polyethylene pipe laid on the soil that seeps water by gravity), not drip irrigation under plastic mulch; it is described by the authors as a new method that combines drip and mulch. Nutrient availability is not measured at all. Per the rating rules this is a technology mismatch, so Q2 is no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own two-year field experiment on water pillow vs furrow irrigation of soybean with measured yield, water use and soil temperature.
rows.notes: The study reports no weed counts, weed biomass or herbicide-use data of its own. Weed suppression is only attributed to the mulching effect by citing B<U+00FC>k<U+00FC>n et al. In addition, the technology tested is a water-pillow pipe, not drip irrigation under plastic mulch, so this is also a technology mismatch.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a primary field experiment on water pillow (WP) irrigation, a gravity-fed perforated black polyethylene pipe acting as both emitter and mulch, compared to furrow irrigation for soybean in Sanliurfa, Turkey (2003 and 2006). Both claim rows concern drip irrigation under plastic mulch (DIPM), which the rating instructions explicitly identify as a technology mismatch for water-pillow studies.
